words.definition: A person who habitually doubts or questions accepted claims and beliefs.
words.example: As a lifelong skeptic, she refused to accept the miracle cure until she saw hard proof.
words.mnemonic: Skeptic → 'skip-tick': someone who skips ticking the 'I believe it' box.

words.definition: Too willing to accept things as true without asking for proof.
words.example: The credulous investor handed over his savings after a single smooth phone pitch.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'credit' (Latin credere, to believe) — you give belief on credit.

words.definition: Easily tricked or deceived because of trusting people too readily.
words.example: So gullible was he that he bought a bridge from a stranger on the street.
words.mnemonic: A gullible person is like a gull (seagull) that swallows anything tossed to it.

words.definition: Feeling uncertain, or seeming unreliable and not worthy of trust.
words.example: She gave the salesman a dubious look before slowly backing out of the deal.
words.mnemonic: 'Du' echoes 'duo/double' — when dubious you are of two minds.

words.definition: Unwilling or unable to accept that something is true.
words.example: He stared at the lottery ticket, incredulous that the numbers actually matched.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + cred (believe): not believing — the flip side of credulous.

words.definition: Having more than one possible meaning and therefore unclear.
words.example: Her ambiguous reply left us unsure whether she had said yes or no.
words.mnemonic: ambi- means 'both' (as in ambidextrous) — the phrase points both ways at once.

words.definition: To speak vaguely on purpose so as to avoid committing or telling the truth.
words.example: When asked who broke the vase, the boy equivocated until his mother demanded a straight answer.
words.mnemonic: equi (equal) + voc (voice): giving equal voice to both sides so you pledge to neither.

words.definition: Open to more than one interpretation and therefore uncertain.
words.example: The test results were equivocal, so the doctor ordered a second scan to be sure.
words.mnemonic: Same root as equivocate: equal (equi) voices (voc) — a meaning that could go either way.

words.definition: To become unsteady or unsure and hesitate between choices.
words.example: Her confidence began to waver as the crowd fell silent and stared.
words.mnemonic: A flag wavers in the wind, swinging back and forth, never fixed — so does an unsure mind.

words.definition: To act nervously and be unable to reach a decision.
words.example: Stop dithering and pick a restaurant — we've been standing here twenty minutes!
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'hither-thither' — you rush hither and thither and get nowhere.

words.definition: Not certain or fixed; done as a trial and open to change.
words.example: We've made tentative plans for Friday, but nothing is confirmed yet.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'tent': a tent is temporary and easily taken down, just like these plans.

words.definition: An opinion or guess formed without solid evidence.
words.example: Without any data, his theory about the crash was pure conjecture.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + ject (throw, as in 'eject'): ideas thrown together into a guess.

words.definition: To conclude or guess something from very little evidence.
words.example: From the muddy boots by the door, she surmised that he had been hiking.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sir, my eyes': from what my eyes catch, I make my guess.

words.definition: To suppose that something is true without having proof.
words.example: I presume you've eaten, since the kitchen light was on when I arrived.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + sume (take): you take it as true before the proof arrives.

words.definition: To state firmly and confidently that something is true.
words.example: The witness continued to aver that she had seen the defendant leave at midnight.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'ver' (Latin verus, true, as in 'verify') — to declare as the truth.

words.definition: Refusing absolutely to change a decision or opinion, no matter the pressure.
words.example: Despite hours of pleading, she remained adamant that no one would leave before the work was finished.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a diamond' — the hardest stone, impossible to bend, scratch, or wear down.

words.definition: Firmly determined to follow through on a purpose despite difficulty.
words.example: The climbers were resolute, pressing upward through the storm even as others turned back.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'resolve' inside it — a resolute person has made a resolution and won't let it drop.

words.definition: Very loyal and firmly committed in one's support or attitude.
words.example: A staunch defender of the library, he attended every council meeting to protest its closure.
words.mnemonic: To 'staunch' also means to stop a flow of blood — a staunch ally stands firm like a dam, holding back trouble.

words.definition: Firm and unwavering in loyalty, purpose, or conviction.
words.example: Through every setback, her steadfast support of the project never once flickered.
words.mnemonic: 'Steady' + 'fast' (as in 'held fast') — standing steady and held fast in one place.

words.definition: Feeling cautious and alert about possible danger or trouble.
words.example: After being cheated once, he grew wary of any deal that seemed too generous.
words.mnemonic: 'Wary' sits inside 'beware' — both warn you to watch out.

words.definition: Cautiously reluctant to do something, especially to give or risk it.
words.example: The editor was chary of praise, handing it out only when a piece truly earned it.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'care-y' — full of care; it's just 'wary' with a C.

words.definition: Distrustful and suspicious of someone or something.
words.example: Investors were leery of the startup after its founder dodged every hard question.
words.mnemonic: You give it a 'leer' — a sidelong, suspicious look at what you don't trust.

words.definition: A feeling of doubt or worry about a future outcome or decision.
words.example: She signed the contract despite a nagging misgiving that the terms were too good to be true.
words.mnemonic: 'Mis-' (wrong, as in mistake) + 'giving' — your gut is 'giving' you a warning that something is wrong.

words.definition: A brief pang of doubt or unease, often about whether an act is right.
words.example: He pocketed the extra change without a single qualm.
words.mnemonic: It looks like 'calm' with a Q wedged in — a qualm is the thing that disturbs your calm.

words.definition: A state of uncertainty over what to do in a tricky situation.
words.example: Offered both jobs on the same day, she found herself in a real quandary.
words.mnemonic: 'Quandary' ≈ 'quarry' + 'wonder' — stuck wondering, trapped in a pit of choices.

words.definition: Impossible to question or deny; utterly certain.
words.example: The fingerprints on the glass were indubitable proof that he had been in the room.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'dubitable' (from Latin 'dubium', doubt) — literally not able to be doubted.

words.definition: Expressed so clearly and firmly that no doubt or ambiguity remains.
words.example: Her answer was an unequivocal no, and she repeated it without softening a word.
words.mnemonic: 'Equi-' (equal) + 'voc' (voice): equivocal means speaking with two equal voices — add 'un-' and there's only one, plain meaning.

words.definition: Stated absolutely, with no conditions, exceptions, or hedging.
words.example: The minister issued a categorical denial, insisting there had been no meeting at all.
words.mnemonic: Think 'category' — a categorical statement drops something firmly into one box, no in-between.

words.definition: Expressed with force and clear stress to show strong feeling.
words.example: With an emphatic slam of the door, she made her anger impossible to miss.
words.mnemonic: 'Emphasis' lives inside it — an emphatic remark is delivered with heavy emphasis.

words.definition: Insisting on instant obedience and allowing no refusal or discussion.
words.example: With a peremptory wave, the general dismissed the officers before they could speak.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'preempt' — a peremptory order preempts any argument, shutting it down at once.

words.definition: Behaving in a proud, controlling way that expects instant obedience from others.
words.example: With an imperious wave of her hand, the manager silenced the room and demanded the report at once.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'imperial' — picture an emperor barking orders that everyone must obey.

words.definition: A statement accepted as obviously true without needing any proof.
words.example: In geometry class we started from a single axiom that no one bothered to question or prove.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'axios' (worthy) — an idea so worthy of trust it stands on its own.

words.definition: A formal pronouncement made with authority, or a well-known saying.
words.example: The old coach lived by the dictum that practice matters more than talent.
words.mnemonic: Root 'dic-' means to say (dictate, diction) — a dictum is something dictated from on high.

words.definition: A core belief or principle held by a person or group.
words.example: Honesty in every transaction is a central tenet of the family business.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tenere' (to hold) — picture a 'ten net' that holds your beliefs safely.

words.definition: A short formal declaration of the beliefs that guide someone's life.
words.example: His personal credo, printed above his desk, read: leave every place better than you found it.
words.mnemonic: Latin for 'I believe' — the same 'cred-' root as credit, what you give your faith to.

words.definition: Widely repeated but probably untrue or of doubtful origin.
words.example: The tale that Einstein failed math is apocryphal, repeated everywhere yet backed by no records.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'apokryphos' (hidden away) — 'a-pocket-full' of stories with no real source behind them.

words.definition: Fake or based on false reasoning, though appearing genuine.
words.example: The salesman's spurious claims about the pill's cure collapsed under a single lab test.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spur' — a spur-of-the-moment lie dressed up to look real.

words.definition: The quality of being truthful and accurate.
words.example: The jury weighed the witness's veracity before trusting a word of the testimony.
words.mnemonic: Root 'ver-' means true (verify, verdict) — a 'VERy' honest quality.

words.definition: Acceptance of something as true or believable.
words.example: New satellite images lent credence to reports the villagers had made for years.
words.mnemonic: Same 'cred-' root as credit — to give credence is to give something your credit or trust.

words.definition: Able to be believed; convincing and trustworthy.
words.example: Her calm, detailed account made her the most credible witness the detective had interviewed.
words.mnemonic: 'Cred-' (believe) — someone with good 'credentials' is worth believing.

words.definition: Seeming reasonable or likely to be true, though perhaps not.
words.example: His excuse for the missing money sounded plausible until the receipts told another story.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'applause' — an argument smooth enough to earn a clap, whether or not it's right.

words.definition: Able to be defended against attack or objection.
words.example: Once the data leaked, the company's official story was no longer tenable.
words.mnemonic: From 'tenere' (to hold) — read it as 'ten-able,' a position strong enough to hold for ten rounds.

words.definition: To think carefully and at length about something.
words.example: He sat by the window to cogitate on the offer, weighing every risk before replying.
words.mnemonic: Picture mental 'cogs' turning — the gears of your brain grinding through a hard problem.

words.definition: To consider something thoughtfully before deciding.
words.example: She paused to ponder the question, unwilling to answer until she had thought it through.
words.mnemonic: Shares roots with 'ponderous' (weighty) — you weigh the options in your mind.

words.definition: To turn something over slowly in your mind again and again.
words.example: For weeks he continued to ruminate on the argument, replaying it long after everyone else forgot.
words.mnemonic: A cow (a ruminant) chews its cud over and over — you chew the same thought repeatedly.

words.definition: To weigh options and think carefully before reaching a decision.
words.example: The jury withdrew to deliberate for three days before returning a verdict.
words.mnemonic: de-LIBRA-te: picture the scales of Libra, weighing each choice before you commit.

words.definition: To struggle awkwardly and helplessly, unsure how to proceed.
words.example: Handed a question he hadn't prepared for, the candidate floundered at the podium.
words.mnemonic: A flounder is a flatfish — picture it flopping and thrashing helplessly on the deck.

words.definition: Overstepping proper limits by taking more liberty than is warranted.
words.example: It was presumptuous of him to sit at the head of the table in a stranger's home.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + sume (take): someone who takes liberties before earning the right.

words.definition: To seize or claim something for oneself without any right to it.
words.example: The deputy arrogated powers that clearly belonged to the elected board.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'arrogant' inside it — an arrogant person grabs authority that isn't theirs.

words.definition: To declare or admit something openly and without shame.
words.example: She avowed her support for the strike in front of the entire factory floor.
words.mnemonic: a-VOW: to make a vow out loud, declaring it for everyone to hear.

words.definition: To state something earnestly and solemnly as absolutely true.
words.example: The accused asseverated his innocence, swearing on everything he held dear.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'severe': you make the claim with severe, solemn seriousness.

words.definition: To assume something as true to serve as a starting point for reasoning.
words.example: Euclid postulated that a straight line can be drawn between any two points.
words.mnemonic: A 'post' is a pole you plant firmly in the ground as your starting assumption.

words.definition: To form opinions or guesses about something without solid evidence.
words.example: Reporters speculated for weeks about who would be named the new director.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'spectacles' (specere, to look): you peer ahead and guess.

words.definition: To estimate unknown values by extending a known pattern or trend.
words.example: From three months of sales, she extrapolated the revenue for the full year.
words.mnemonic: extra + (inter)polate: you go 'extra,' beyond the data you have, to project further.

words.definition: To reach a conclusion from evidence and reasoning rather than direct statement.
words.example: From the muddy boots by the door, she inferred he had been walking in the fields.
words.mnemonic: in + ferre (to carry): you carry a conclusion INto your mind from the clues.

words.definition: To draw a specific conclusion by reasoning logically from general facts.
words.example: From the unbroken lock, the detective deduced that the thief must have had a key.
words.mnemonic: de- (down) + ducere (to lead): logic leads you down, step by step, to the answer.

words.definition: To support a statement or theory with extra evidence that confirms it.
words.example: A second witness corroborated her account of the accident down to the timing.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'robor' (Latin robur, strength): you add strength to someone's claim.

words.definition: To prove the truth of a claim by providing solid evidence.
words.example: He could not substantiate his expenses without the receipts he had lost.
words.mnemonic: Give 'substance' to a claim so it stands up as something real.

words.definition: To confirm that something is accurate, sound, or officially acceptable.
words.example: The lab results validated the new drug's effect on blood pressure.
words.mnemonic: From Latin validus, 'strong': you show that the thing holds up and is valid.

words.definition: To prove that a statement or argument is false or mistaken.
words.example: New forensic evidence refuted the theory that the fire had been accidental.
words.mnemonic: From Latin refutare, 'to drive back': picture a fencer parrying and driving the argument back.

words.definition: To prove a claim wrong by offering opposing evidence or reasoning.
words.example: In her closing statement, the defense attorney rebutted every point the prosecution had raised.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-butt' — you butt the opposing argument right back at it.

words.definition: To declare a statement false or to oppose it openly in words.
words.example: No one on the crew dared gainsay the old captain's account of the storm.
words.mnemonic: 'gain' comes from Old English for 'against' + 'say' — to say against someone.

words.definition: To assert the opposite of what someone else has stated.
words.example: His lavish spending contradicts everything he preaches about thrift and saving.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'contra' (against) + 'dicere' (to speak) — literally to speak against.

words.definition: To dispute or argue against the truth of a statement or idea.
words.example: The newly discovered fossils controvert the long-accepted theory of the species' origin.
words.mnemonic: 'contra' (against) + 'vert' (turn) — to turn against; the root inside 'controversy'.

words.definition: To show through evidence that a claim or belief is false.
words.example: A single counterexample was enough to disprove the mathematician's bold conjecture.
words.mnemonic: 'dis-' (not) attached to the idea of proving — it undoes a proof.

words.definition: To expose the falseness of a myth, claim, or popular belief.
words.example: The documentary set out to debunk the wild conspiracy theories about the moon landing.
words.mnemonic: 'de-' (remove) + 'bunk' (nonsense) — to take the bunk out of a claim.

words.definition: To prove a person or their argument to be wrong.
words.example: With three well-chosen examples the professor calmly confuted the student's entire thesis.
words.mnemonic: Blend of 'confuse' and 'refute' — you refute them so thoroughly they're left confounded.

words.definition: To give a false impression of something, or to contradict and prove untrue.
words.example: Her calm voice seemed to belie the panic she must have felt as the plane shuddered.
words.mnemonic: Hear the word "lie" inside be-LIE — to belie is to make something into a lie, to misrepresent it.

words.definition: To act or go against a law, rule, or established principle.
words.example: Building a factory on the marsh would contravene the town's conservation ordinance.
words.mnemonic: 'contra' (against) + 'venire' (to come) — to come up against a rule.

words.definition: To reject or refuse to accept something as valid or binding.
words.example: The scientist publicly repudiated the fraudulent study that had been published under her name.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'reputation' inside it — you push something away to protect your reputation.

words.definition: To deny any knowledge of, responsibility for, or support for something.
words.example: The senator quickly disavowed the extremist group that had endorsed his campaign.
words.mnemonic: 'dis-' (not) + 'avow' (to declare openly) — the opposite of vowing you're behind it.

words.definition: To formally withdraw a former belief or statement, often in public.
words.example: Under threat of prison, Galileo was forced to recant his claim that the Earth moves.
words.mnemonic: 're-' (back) + 'cant' (to chant/sing) — to sing your words back and take them in.

words.definition: To take back a statement or promise as if it were never made.
words.example: The newspaper retracted the story after discovering its source had fabricated everything.
words.mnemonic: 're-' (back) + 'tract' (to pull) — to pull back, like a cat's retractable claws.

words.definition: To go back on a promise, agreement, or commitment.
words.example: The company reneged on its pledge to raise wages once profits had recovered.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-negate' — you negate the word you gave earlier.

words.definition: To speak or write vaguely, avoiding a firm decision or opinion.
words.example: Asked whether he would support the bill, the candidate waffled for a full ten minutes.
words.mnemonic: Picture a waffle — full of holes and squishy, with no firm center to it.

words.definition: To avoid a clear commitment by qualifying or protecting a statement or bet.
words.example: When asked if he'd finish by Friday, he hedged, saying it all depended.
words.mnemonic: A hedge is a bushy fence you hide behind — to hedge is to hide behind vague words.

words.definition: To stall or delay a decision in order to gain more time.
words.example: The negotiators temporized for weeks, hoping the crisis would resolve before they had to choose.
words.mnemonic: TEMPOrize hides 'tempo' (time) — you buy time by slowing the tempo.

words.definition: To speak or act evasively so as to avoid telling the truth.
words.example: Under cross-examination the witness began to prevaricate, giving answers that never quite matched the facts.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pre-various' — offering various shifting stories instead of one straight truth.

words.definition: To hide one's real feelings or intentions behind a false appearance.
words.example: She dissembled her disappointment, smiling warmly as her rival accepted the award.
words.mnemonic: Dis-ASSEMBLE the truth — take it apart so no one sees the real thing.

words.definition: To pretend to have a feeling, state, or reaction that is not real.
words.example: He feigned illness to skip the meeting, coughing dramatically until his boss sent him home.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'reign' — a pretender feigns the throne he doesn't truly hold.

words.definition: Appearing or claimed to be true on the surface, though possibly not genuine.
words.example: The ostensible reason for the visit was business, but everyone knew he came to see her.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'ostentatious' (Latin ostendere, to show) — it's what's shown outwardly.

words.definition: Commonly assumed or reputed to be something, without firm proof.
words.example: The putative author of the anonymous letter denied ever having held a pen to it.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'putare', to reckon — people reckon it's so; picture 'putting' a label on someone.

words.definition: Claimed or rumored to be so, but not confirmed as fact.
words.example: Police examined the purported confession, unsure whether the defendant had actually written it.
words.mnemonic: It 'purports to' — think of someone reporting a claim they can't back up.

words.definition: Existing only as an idea or in theory rather than in reality.
words.example: The budget listed a notional figure for repairs, a placeholder no one expected to be exact.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'NOTION' — it lives only as a notion, an idea in the head.

words.definition: Based on a supposed situation rather than an actual or proven one.
words.example: The lawyer posed a hypothetical: what if the driver had swerved instead of braking?
words.mnemonic: Holds 'hypothesis' — a proposed 'what-if' you test, not a settled fact.

words.definition: Open to argument, or no longer having any practical relevance.
words.example: Once the funding was cancelled, the debate over the design became moot.
words.mnemonic: In 'moot court' students argue undecided cases — endlessly debatable yet leading nowhere.

words.definition: Likely to cause disagreement or provoke heated argument.
words.example: Immigration remained the most contentious issue of the debate, splitting the room in two.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'con-TENSE-ious' — full of tension; people contend and contest over it.

words.definition: Open to question or disagreement; not clearly established as true.
words.example: It is arguable whether the new policy helped anyone, since the data points both ways.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'argue' + 'able' — it's something you could argue either way.

words.definition: Having a hidden or puzzling meaning that is hard to understand.
words.example: She left a cryptic note that read only 'the third stair knows,' and vanished.
words.mnemonic: From 'crypt', a hidden underground vault — the meaning is buried, like a cryptogram.

words.definition: Difficult to interpret or understand; mysteriously puzzling.
words.example: The Mona Lisa's enigmatic smile has intrigued viewers for centuries.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'ENIGMA' — like the Enigma code machine no one could crack.
